1. PREMISE: Your framing treats the frequency of requests as primarily a problem of others' insufficient effort or capability. The hidden assumption is that you occupy a neutral position—that your accessibility, demonstrated competence, and family role have not actively shaped the pattern you now experience. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that you have trained the people around you, through consistent availability and performance, to route problems to you as the path of least resistance, regardless of their actual capacity to solve those problems.

2. STAKES: Your family members stand to lose direct experience solving problems, learning from failure, and developing confidence in their own judgment—outcomes that compound over years. Your employer or clients stand to lose productivity and focus during periods when you are mentally diverted by external demands. Your own health stands to lose continuity of attention, sleep quality, and stress levels during high-concentration work phases. The people requesting favors stand to gain immediate solutions but at the cost of dependency and stunted capability.

3. DIRECTIVE: Establish a fixed, narrow window—one hour per week, at a scheduled time you announce in advance—during which you will address non-emergency requests, and decline all requests outside that window without explanation or apology. The decisive reason is that availability shapes demand more powerfully than any verbal boundary; only scarcity teaches people to filter their own requests and solve their own problems first.
[Rejected path: explaining why each request is unreasonable or telling people you are busy. This communicates that you are available if the request passes a threshold test of legitimacy; probability of primary harm: high.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Establish a single recurring hour each week, announced to all parties, at which point you will address requests—and refuse all requests arising outside that interval without providing reasons. When you withhold explanation, you remove the opportunity for negotiation, reframing, or appeals to your sympathy; requests will decline sharply once requesters discover that effort spent persuading you produces zero return. The alternative position—that refusing requests harms relationships—fails because relationships that depend on your constant availability are not relationships; they are dependencies that prevent the other person from developing the judgment and capability that sustain real connection. You will experience discomfort during the transition as people test your boundary; this discomfort is the cost of teaching others that you are a finite resource. Therefore: announce your fixed weekly availability window and refuse all requests outside it without elaboration or exception.
